questions.stem: What is the definition of a fuel?

options.text: A substance that releases heat energy when it burns
options.explanation: Heat output on burning is the whole definition, with burning itself exothermic.

options.text: Any liquid that can be poured into an engine
options.explanation: Solid coal is a fuel too; physical state is not part of the definition.

options.text: A substance that absorbs heat as it reacts
options.explanation: Fuels give heat out; absorbing heat is the endothermic opposite.

options.text: Any substance containing carbon
options.explanation: Carbon content alone does not make a fuel; the heat release on burning does.

questions.stem: Which list contains only fossil fuels?

options.text: Coal, oil and natural gas
options.explanation: These three head the fossil fuel list, joined by oil shales and tar sands.

options.text: Coal, ethanol and natural gas
options.explanation: Ethanol is not a fossil fuel on this list; it belongs to the alcohols family.

options.text: Wood, oil and bitumen
options.explanation: Wood is not a fossil fuel; it is recent plant material.

options.text: Peat, hydrogen and oil
options.explanation: Hydrogen is not fossil; the fossil set is coal, oil, gas, shales and tar sands.

questions.stem: What are the products of the complete combustion of propane, C3H8?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
options.explanation: Excess oxygen turns all three carbons into CO2 and all eight hydrogens into water.

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water
options.explanation: CO appears only when oxygen is limited; complete burning goes all the way to CO2.

options.text: Carbon and steam only
options.explanation: Plain carbon is the soot of incomplete burning, not the complete case.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide and water
options.explanation: Propane itself carries no sulfur; SO2 comes from impurities in other fuels.
Three carbon atoms in propane must all appear as three CO2 molecules on the right.
One CO2 would strand two of the three carbons from propane.
Five belongs to the oxygen coefficient; the carbon count fixes the CO2 at three.
Eight counts hydrogens, not carbon dioxide molecules.

questions.stem: Why do fossil fuels all contain small quantities of sulfur?

options.text: Because sulfur impurities are present in the fuel sources themselves
options.explanation: The crude and coal carry traces of sulfur from their formation, which survives into the refined fuel.

options.text: Because sulfur is added deliberately during refining
options.explanation: Nothing is added; the sulfur is an unwanted leftover from the source material.

options.text: Because engines manufacture sulfur during use
options.explanation: Engines only release what the fuel already contains.

options.text: Because sulfur dissolves out of the air into the fuel
options.explanation: The sulfur comes with the fuel from the ground, not from the air afterwards.

questions.stem: Which condition causes incomplete combustion in a boiler?

options.text: Insufficient oxygen reaching the flame
options.explanation: Starved flames cannot fully oxidise the carbon, so CO and soot appear.

options.text: Excess oxygen reaching the flame
options.explanation: Excess oxygen drives the complete reaction to CO2 and water instead.

options.text: The presence of water vapour in the air
options.explanation: Water vapour is a product of burning, not a cause of incomplete burning.

options.text: Using methane instead of propane
options.explanation: Any hydrocarbon burns incompletely if oxygen is short; the fuel choice is not the cause.

questions.stem: In the equation 2CH4 + 3O2 -> 2CO + 4H2O, why does only 3O2 appear instead of 4O2?

options.text: Because the limited oxygen cannot fully oxidise the carbon to dioxide
options.explanation: Three O2 is all the supply allows, so carbon stops at monoxide and the equation reflects the shortage.

options.text: Because methane contains less carbon when oxygen is scarce
options.explanation: The methane formula never changes; only the oxygen supply changes.

options.text: Because water needs no oxygen at all
options.explanation: Every water molecule carries an oxygen atom, which is part of the same budget.

options.text: Because the 3 balances the equation more neatly
options.explanation: Coefficients follow atom counts, not tidiness; the 3 records the real oxygen limit.

questions.stem: What is soot, in the language of this note?

options.text: Unburnt fuel appearing as carbon particles
options.explanation: Soot is the carbon that never found enough oxygen to leave as an oxide.

options.text: Ash from the minerals in the fuel
options.explanation: The note names soot as unburnt hydrocarbon, not mineral ash.

options.text: Another name for water vapour
options.explanation: Water is a separate, fully oxidised product; soot is carbon.

options.text: The catalyst used inside engines
options.explanation: Catalysts are separate hardware; soot is a combustion product.

questions.stem: Methane burns with equation CH4 + O2 -> C + 2H2O. What does this show about the oxygen supply?

options.text: The supply is so poor that carbon cannot oxidise at all
options.explanation: Carbon emerges as the bare element, the bottom rung of the incomplete ladder.

options.text: The supply is generous, so burning is complete
options.explanation: Complete burning would show CO2, not bare carbon, on the right.

options.text: The supply is irrelevant to this equation
options.explanation: The one-oxygen supply is exactly what forces the carbon product down to C.

options.text: The methane has decomposed without burning
options.explanation: The reaction still burns the hydrogen to water; it is incomplete burning, not mere breakdown.

questions.stem: Why does incomplete combustion matter beyond the equation?

options.text: Because carbon monoxide formed this way is poisonous to people
options.explanation: The next section shows CO binding in the blood; the equation is where the danger starts.

options.text: Because soot makes the water products acidic
options.explanation: Soot is carbon; the acid-rain story belongs to sulfur and nitrogen oxides.

options.text: Because incomplete burning releases no energy
options.explanation: Heat is still released, just less efficiently than complete burning.

options.text: Because boilers stop working entirely
options.explanation: Appliances keep running; the hazard is the gas released, not a shutdown.

questions.stem: Why is carbon monoxide especially dangerous in the home?

options.text: It is odourless, colourless and tasteless, so it goes unnoticed
options.explanation: With no sensory warning, a person can inhale it without realising anything is present.

options.text: It has a strong smell that people ignore
options.explanation: The danger is the absence of smell, not the ignoring of one.

options.text: It stains walls green as a warning
options.explanation: CO is colourless and leaves no visible trace to warn anyone.

options.text: It explodes on contact with air
options.explanation: The hazard is poisoning through inhalation, not explosion.

questions.stem: According to the specification, what is the key point about carbon monoxide poisoning?

options.text: It reduces the capacity of the blood to transport oxygen
options.explanation: The exam hint names exactly this as the marking point examiners look for.

options.text: It dissolves the walls of the lungs
options.explanation: The mechanism is oxygen transport, not physical damage to lung tissue.

options.text: It thickens the blood until it cannot flow
options.explanation: Flow thickness is not the claim; carrying capacity is.

options.text: It prevents red blood cells from being made
options.explanation: Existing cells are hijacked; production of new cells is not part of the story.

questions.stem: How much more strongly does haemoglobin bind carbon monoxide than oxygen?

options.text: Around 200 to 250 times more strongly
options.explanation: The detailed explanation quotes that range as the affinity gap.

options.text: About the same strength
options.explanation: If the strengths matched, CO would be far less dangerous than it is.

options.text: About half as strongly
options.explanation: CO binds far more strongly than oxygen, not more weakly.

options.text: Around 2 to 5 times more strongly
options.explanation: The gap is two orders of magnitude larger, which is why CO wins so completely.

questions.stem: What name is given to the stable compound formed when haemoglobin binds CO?

options.text: Carboxyhaemoglobin
options.explanation: The detailed explanation names carboxyhaemoglobin as the stable product of the binding.

options.text: Oxyhaemoglobin
options.explanation: That is the oxygen-carrying form CO prevents from forming.

options.text: Carboxylic acid
options.explanation: That is an organic acid family, unrelated to the blood compound here.

options.text: Carbonic acid
options.explanation: Carbonic acid belongs to CO2 in water, a different gas and a different story.

questions.stem: Is referring to haemoglobin required in your exam answer?

options.text: No, but recent mark schemes accept it if the oxygen-transport point is stated
options.explanation: The spec excludes the requirement, yet mark schemes allow the detail alongside the key point.

options.text: Yes, the full haemoglobin mechanism must be quoted
options.explanation: The specification explicitly says references to haemoglobin are not required.

options.text: No, and mentioning haemoglobin loses the mark
options.explanation: Mark schemes accept it; only the key point must not be omitted.

options.text: Only for extended writing questions
options.explanation: The rule does not switch with question type; the key point is always the target.
